title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: At dawn on November 16th, Denisov's squadron — the one in which Nicholas Rostov served, part of Prince Bagration's detachment — moved out from where it had spent the night and advanced into action as planned. After marching behind other columns for about two-thirds of a mile, they were stopped on the main road. Rostov watched the Cossacks pass by, then the first and second squadrons of hussars, then infantry battalions and artillery, and finally Generals Bagration and Dolgorukov riding past with their adjutants. All the fear he'd felt before battle, all his inner struggle to conquer that fear, all his dreams of proving himself a true hussar — it had all been for nothing. Their squadron was held in reserve, and Nicholas Rostov spent the day in a miserable, frustrated mood. At nine in the morning he heard gunfire ahead and shouts of "Hurrah!" and saw wounded men being carried back (not many of them), and eventually watched as a whole detachment of French cavalry was brought in under Cossack escort. The engagement was clearly over — small but successful. The men and officers returning spoke of a brilliant victory, the capture of the town of Wischau, and the seizure of an entire French squadron. The day was bright and sunny after a sharp overnight frost, and the cheerful autumn light matched the mood of victory, which was conveyed not just by the stories of those who had fought, but by the joyful expressions on the faces of soldiers, officers, generals, and adjutants passing Rostov in both directions. And Nicholas, who had suffered all the dread of anticipation for nothing and spent that fine day doing nothing, felt even more depressed.
[speaking in French] "Come here, Rostov. Let's drink to drown our sorrows!" shouted Denisov, who had settled by the roadside with a flask and some food.
The officers gathered around Denisov's canteen, eating and talking.
"Look! They're bringing in another one!" cried one of the officers, pointing at a captured French dragoon being led in on foot by two Cossacks.
One of the Cossacks was leading a fine, large French horse by the bridle — taken from the prisoner.
"Sell us that horse!" Denisov called out to the Cossacks.
"If you like, your honor!"

The officers got up and gathered around the Cossacks and their prisoner. The French dragoon was a young man from Alsace who spoke French with a German accent. He was breathless with agitation, his face was red, and as soon as he heard French being spoken he started talking rapidly to the officers, turning from one to another. He said he wouldn't have been captured — it wasn't his fault but the corporal's, who had sent him to fetch some horse blankets even though he'd warned him the Russians were there. And with every other sentence he added: "But don't hurt my little horse!" and stroked the animal. It was obvious he hadn't fully grasped his situation. One moment he was apologizing for getting captured, the next he was acting as if he were standing before his own commanding officers, insisting on his military discipline and dedication. He brought with him into the Russian rearguard all the freshness and atmosphere of the French army, which felt completely foreign to them.
The Cossacks sold the horse for two gold pieces, and Rostov, now the richest officer in the group after receiving his money, bought it.
"But don't hurt my little horse!" said the Alsatian good-naturedly to Rostov when the animal was handed over to the hussar.
Rostov smiled reassuringly at the dragoon and gave him money.
"Move along! Move along!" said the Cossack, tapping the prisoner's arm to get him walking.
"The Emperor! The Emperor!" The cry suddenly ran through the hussars.

Everyone began running about and getting into position, and Rostov saw several riders approaching from up the road behind him, white plumes in their hats. In an instant every man was in his place, waiting.

Rostov didn't know or remember how he ran to his position and mounted his horse. Instantly his regret at missing the action was gone, his dreary mood among people he was tired of had vanished, and every thought of himself had disappeared. He was filled with happiness at being near the Emperor. He felt this closeness alone made up for the entire wasted day. He was as happy as a lover at the long-awaited moment of reunion. Not daring to look around, and without looking around, he was ecstatically aware of the Emperor's approach. He sensed it not just from the sound of approaching hooves but because as the Emperor drew nearer, everything around him grew brighter, more joyful, more meaningful, more festive. That sun, radiating its mild and majestic light, came closer and closer, and already Rostov felt himself wrapped in its glow. He heard the Emperor's voice — that kind, calm, majestic voice that was at the same time so simple! And as if in harmony with Rostov's feelings, a deathlike stillness fell, broken only by the Emperor's words.
"The Pavlograd hussars?" he asked.
"The reserves, sire!" replied a voice — a very human one compared to the voice that had said "The Pavlograd hussars?"

The Emperor drew level with Rostov and stopped. Alexander's face was even more beautiful than it had been three days earlier at the review. It glowed with such cheerfulness and youth, such innocent youthfulness, that it resembled a lively fourteen-year-old boy — and yet it was the face of the Emperor himself. While casually surveying the squadron, his eyes met Rostov's and rested on them for no more than two seconds. Whether or not the Emperor understood what was happening in Rostov's heart (it seemed to Rostov that he understood everything), his light-blue eyes gazed into Rostov's face for about two seconds. A gentle, soft light poured from them. Then suddenly he raised his eyebrows, touched his horse sharply with his left foot, and galloped on.

The young Emperor had been unable to resist his desire to be present at the battle, and despite the objections of his courtiers, had left the third column at noon and galloped toward the front lines. Before he reached the hussars, several adjutants had already met him with news of the successful action.

This battle — which amounted to the capture of a French squadron — was portrayed as a brilliant victory over the French, and so the Emperor and the entire army, especially while smoke still hung over the battlefield, believed the French had been defeated and were retreating against their will. A few minutes after the Emperor rode past, the Pavlograd division was ordered to advance. In Wischau itself, a small German town, Rostov saw the Emperor again. In the market square, where there had been fairly heavy fighting before the Emperor arrived, several dead and wounded soldiers lay where they had fallen — there hadn't been time to move them. The Emperor, surrounded by his officers and courtiers, was riding a bob-tailed chestnut mare — a different horse from the one at the review — and leaning to one side, he gracefully held a gold lorgnette to his eyes and looked down at a soldier lying face-down, blood on his bare head. The wounded man was so dirty, rough, and disfigured that his closeness to the Emperor shocked Rostov. Rostov saw how the Emperor's rounded shoulders shuddered as though a chill ran through them, how his left foot began involuntarily tapping the horse's side with the spur, and how the well-trained horse glanced around unconcerned and didn't move. An adjutant dismounted and lifted the soldier under the arms to place him on a stretcher that had been brought up. The soldier groaned.
"Gently, gently! Can't you do it more carefully?" said the Emperor, apparently suffering more than the dying soldier himself, and he rode away.
Rostov saw tears filling the Emperor's eyes and heard him say to Czartoryski as he rode off: "What a terrible thing war is — what a terrible thing!"

The vanguard troops were positioned in front of Wischau, within sight of the enemy's lines, which had given ground all day at the slightest exchange of fire. The Emperor's gratitude was announced to the vanguard, rewards were promised, and the men received a double ration of vodka. The campfires crackled and the soldiers' songs rang out even louder than the night before. Denisov was celebrating his promotion to major, and Rostov, who had already drunk plenty, proposed a toast to the Emperor at the end of the feast. "Not 'our Sovereign, the Emperor,' the way they say it at official dinners," he said, "but to the health of our Sovereign — that good, wonderful, and great man! Let's drink to his health and to the certain defeat of the French!"

"If we fought the way we did before," he continued, "not letting the French through, like at Schon Grabern — what won't we do now that he himself is leading us? We'll all gladly die for him! Isn't that right, gentlemen? Maybe I'm not saying this perfectly — I've had a lot to drink — but that's how I feel, and I know you feel the same! To the health of Alexander the First! Hurrah!"
"Hurrah!" rang out the enthusiastic voices of the officers.
And the old cavalry captain Kirsten shouted just as enthusiastically and just as sincerely as the twenty-year-old Rostov.

When the officers had drained and smashed their glasses, Kirsten filled new ones and, in his shirtsleeves and breeches, walked glass in hand to the soldiers' bonfires. With his long gray mustache and his white chest showing through his open shirt, he stood in a grand pose by the firelight, waving his raised arm.
"Boys! To our Sovereign, the Emperor, and victory over our enemies! Hurrah!" he bellowed in his bold, old hussar's baritone.
The hussars crowded around and responded with hearty, loud cheers.
Late that night, after everyone had gone their separate ways, Denisov patted his favorite, Rostov, on the shoulder with his short hand.
"Since there's no one to fall in love with on campaign, he's gone and fallen in love with the Tsar," he said.
"Denisov, don't joke about it!" cried Rostov. "It's such an elevated, beautiful feeling, such a..."
"I believe you, I believe you, my friend, and I share it and approve..."
"No, you don't understand!"

And Rostov got up and wandered among the campfires, dreaming of what happiness it would be to die — not saving the Emperor's life (he didn't even dare dream of that), but simply to die before his eyes. He truly was in love with the Tsar, with the glory of Russian arms, and with the hope of future victory. And he wasn't the only one who felt this way during those memorable days before the battle of Austerlitz: nine-tenths of the men in the Russian army were then in love, though less ecstatically, with their Tsar and the glory of Russian arms.
